title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service recorded work meetings and used the audio to train its AI systems, according to allegations in a federal lawsuit. The company's default settings captured conversations from Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, then shared recordings with Otter for machine learning, plaintiffs claim. A checkbox in the privacy policy purported to authorize this practice, but users allege they were not adequately informed that recordings would be collected and used this way.

The failure occurred at the point where consent was gathered. Users report that Otter joined meetings through linked workplace calendars and began recording automatically, creating a gap between what the terms stated and what users understood was happening. Catching this would have required either clearer disclosure before recording started, explicit affirmative consent separate from the privacy policy, or human review of how the default settings affected users who had not actively chosen to participate in AI training.

It is not established whether users were in fact deceived, whether de-identification was or was not effective, or whether the company violated the laws cited in the complaint. These are allegations in an ongoing lawsuit.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View tech company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit claims the company's Otter Notebook service, which transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, records conversations by default and shares them with Otter to train its artificial intelligence systems without alerting participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was severely invaded when he discovered recordings of confidential chats were being used this way. The lawsuit claims this violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

Otter.ai has about 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's 2016 founding. While Otter's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for AI training, the lawsuit argues many users are still deceived. Recent complaints on social media describe instances where Otter automatically joined meetings through linked workplace calendars and recorded without consent. Although Otter claims it de-identifies audio before feeding it into machine learning systems, the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information and guarantees anonymity. Otter has denied sharing data with foreign governments or law enforcement.
